newsitem.title: USA: Dollar up on weak Japanese stocks, German job losses.
newsitem.headline: Dollar up on weak Japanese stocks, German job losses.

text.p: The dollar rallied broadly Thursday as fresh signs of economic weakness overseas contrasted with surging stocks and bonds and generally upbeat economic news in the United States.

The dollar rose first against the Japanese yen in Asian trading after the Nikkei 225 stock index plunged more than 3 percent, bringing total losses for the first four trading days of 1997 to nearly 7 percent.
That weakness helped drive investment to U.S. markets, lifting the Dow Jones industrials 76.19 points to a record 6,625.67 and boosting the U.S. 30-year Treasury bond more than a point.
Those gains triggered heavy purchases of dollars for yen, currency traders said.

"What's most significant right now is the relative strength of the U.S. stock market compared to Japan. There seems to be some sort of asset shift going on between the two countries," said Thomas Arnold, chief currency dealer at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank in New York.

Later in the session a report showing German unemployment had risen to a record high in December sent the dollar to a fresh two-year high against the German mark and a 30-month high versus the Swiss franc.

By contrast, economists expected a report Friday to show healthy job growth in the United States. In addition, a report issued Thursday showed wholesale price inflation of only 0.1 percent in the United States in December, bolstering dollar investment.
"People are focusing on many different things, but clearly the dollar overall is moving higher," said Jeffrey Yu, senior currency dealer at Sanwa Bank Ltd. New York.
The dollar rose to 116.37 yen from 115.72 late Wednesday and to 1.5775 marks from 1.5749. The U.S. currency rose to 1.3695 Swiss francs from 1.3645.
The British pound rose to $1.6955 from $1.6880. The dollar stood little changed at Canadian $1.3516 from C$1.3517.
Despite its gains, the dollar failed to hold above 1.58 marks and many traders cited rumours that European central banks had intervened in the market to sell dollars at that level.
As the mark weakens against its European counterparts, exports from other European countries become more expensive, prompting official concern.
"There was decent dollar selling around 1.58 marks and we heard rumours of central bank selling interest up there," said John Beerling, chief currency dealer at Norwest Bank in Minneapolis.
Traders also said an overnight report that U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated his oft-stated desire for a "strong" dollar helped bolster the U.S. currency.
Several Japanese officials earlier in the week publicly warned that the dollar was rising too quickly against the yen, fuelling sharp dollar losses.
But after two days of silence, traders said market players had stopped worrying about potential open-market dollar sales by Japanese authorities.
"Even if Japan were to sell only a modest amount, it could send the dollar much lower and I don't think they want that kind of chaos at this point," Yu said.
